title: Charts and Dashboards That Lead to Decisions
intro: Start from the decision, pick the chart by purpose, then strip it to the data.

topics.title: Charts and Dashboards That Lead to Decisions

learn.title: Chart design rules
learn.text:
• **Label data directly** instead of using a legend
• **Titles state the takeaway** — “Churn rose 3 pts after the price change”
• **Bars start at zero**; lines may not, if the range is obvious
• About **five gridlines**, no more
• **Grey for context, one colour for the point**; five categorical colours at most
• **Never rainbow scales**; red and green only with a second cue
• **Small multiples** with shared scales instead of one crowded chart

try.q: What should a chart title say?
options: The metric and the date range
try.explain: “Churn rose 3 pts after the price change” does the reader's work for them.

learn.title: Dashboard trade-offs
learn.text:
From Bach et al.'s analysis of **144 dashboards and 42 patterns**: four forces trade against each other.

**Screen space** → less room means more **abstraction** → or more **pages** → or more **interaction** (drill-down).

Squeeze one and the stress moves to the others. There is no layout that escapes the trade — only a deliberate choice about which pressure you accept.

try.q: You cut the dashboard to one screen. What happens to the other three forces?
try.explain: Screen space, abstraction, pages and interaction trade against each other.

learn.title: Sometimes the answer isn't a dashboard
learn.text:
If the question has one answer, an **insight** beats a dashboard: a sentence, a number and what to do about it.

Dashboards earn their place when people need to monitor, compare and investigate repeatedly.

And accessibility applies to charts too (Chartability): don't rely on colour alone, make the data available as a table, and check that the chart is navigable without a mouse.

try.q: The team needs the answer to one recurring question. What might serve better than a dashboard?
options: A stated insight with a recommendation
try.explain: “You might not need a dashboard” is one of the findings.

test.q: Why label data directly rather than use a legend?
test.explain: The reader shouldn't have to match colours to names.

test.q: When may a line chart's axis not start at zero?
test.explain: Bars must start at zero; lines are judged differently.

test.q: How many categorical colours at most?
options: As many as the palette provides
test.explain: Grey for context, one colour for the point.

test.q: What did Bach et al. analyse?
test.explain: The source of the four-way trade-off.

test.q: What does red and green always need?
test.explain: Shape, label or position, so colour isn't carrying the meaning alone.
